transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 mins
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Carter (CISO - Heritage), Emily Wong (Dir Cloud), Mark Lewis (Lead Eng)

[00:00] Jordan Reyes: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today. Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. We've got Maya our SE with me. How are you all?
[00:12] Daniel Carter: Good, thanks Jordan. Busy recov, uh, busy afternoon but, um, glad to do this.
[00:18] Emily Wong: Hi all, Emily here. We're primarily focused on compliance and residency questions — quick intro: I'm the director of cloud operations at Heritage.
[00:27] Mark Lewis: Mark — lead eng on our AI infra, hey.
[00:30] Maya Patel: Hi team, Maya here — I'll jump into the technical stuff when needed.
[00:34] Jordan Reyes: Great. Agenda — quick intro, your current stack & constraints, compliance/regulatory must-haves (GDPR/HIPAA/financial controls), and then we'll talk about our Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options and what that means for data residency and logs. Finish with next steps. Sound good?
[00:45] Daniel Carter: Yep. High level: Heritage is rolling out an internal virtual assistant across retail and wealth lines. We need to make sure PII and transactions never leave EU and US boundaries depending on customer. Also, banking regs require audit logs retained but not exported outside our control.
[01:05] Jordan Reyes: Understood. Can you tell us current infra? Are you cloud-first, multi-region?
[01:10] Emily Wong: We're primarily on AWS — prod in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We have strict VPC peering rules and no public subnets for customer data. We use KMS for keys, HSM for certain certs.
[01:20] Mark Lewis: We also run some on-prem for legacy core systems. Latency SLOs for some endpoints are 200ms P95. Cost matters but compliance is hard stop.
[01:30] Maya Patel: Thanks — that clarifies. Two quick Redwood clarifications: our Hosted API is multiregional but can be constrained to regionally isolated endpoints for data residency in many cases; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools under a tenant boundary; Private lets you run our control plane in your VPC or on-prem for full isolation.
[01:50] Daniel Carter: Quick Q — on Hosted, you said "constrained" — is that soft or do you actually guarantee data stays in region?
[01:58] Jordan Reyes: Right now Hosted offers regional routing and strong commitments, but for legally binding guarantees around residency and audit control we typically recommend Dedicated or Private depending on the customer risk profile. Hosted is great for speed to market and cost, but the contract for hard data residency often goes to Dedicated/Private.
[02:18] Emily Wong: If we consider Dedicated, what's the network topology? Do we get a VPC peered instance or is traffic proxied through Redwood?
[02:26] Maya Patel: Dedicated can be deployed two ways: the easiest is a Redwood-managed dedicated cluster that sits in the cloud but with tenant isolation; we can peer or set up private link so traffic never traverses the public internet. For Private, we deploy a customer-managed control plane in your VPC — full peering and no shared control plane.
[02:46] Mark Lewis: On logging — we have policies that prevent raw transcripts or token-level logs from leaving our environment. How granular are your logging controls? Can we redact or disable token-level logging?
[02:56] Maya Patel: Yes, we can configure logging at multiple levels. By default Hosted will capture request/response traces for debugging, but we provide redaction hooks, sampling, and an option to disable full token logging. On Dedicated and Private you can enforce zero exported logs or ship logs to your own S3/logging endpoint where you control retention and access.
[03:18] Daniel Carter: And encryption? We require AES-256 at rest and TLS1.2+ in transit and customer-managed keys for the most sensitive data.
[03:26] Jordan Reyes: We support AES-256 for storage, TLS1.2+ for transit. For KMS we integrate with AWS KMS and HSMs — Dedicated and Private can use customer-managed KMS keys where Redwood does not have the plaintext key.
[03:38] Emily Wong: GDPR question — for EU customers, we need DPAs and SCCs and a way to delete personal data on request. How do deletes work, especially with caches and KV cache?
[03:48] Maya Patel: Good point — we have a deletion workflow. For Hosted, deletion requests can be queued and we scrub KV caches and stored artifacts per SLA; there may be replication windows. For Dedicated/Private you maintain control of persistence and we can set retention policies to ensure you can meet erasure timelines. We also provide DPA and SCC templates.
[04:12] Daniel Carter: HIPAA: we need BAA, audit trails, and ability to restrict any PHI from being logged.
[04:18] Jordan Reyes: We do offer BAAs for enterprise customers — typically Dedicated or Private customers requesting BAA. Hosted can be BAA-eligible on a case by case, but it's rare. Maya do you want to add?
[04:26] Maya Patel: Yeah, generally we see Covered Entities prefer Private or Dedicated because they can control logs, KMS, and where model weights run.
[04:34] Mark Lewis: What about model weights — do you allow custom models or fine-tuning? Do weights ever leave our VPC?
[04:40] Maya Patel: For Private, you can host weights inside your environment. For Dedicated, weights are in the dedicated cluster and aren't shared; we can arrange for model artifacts to be stored in your S3 with encryption. Hosted uses Redwood-managed model repo which is usually outside customer control.
[04:56] Daniel Carter: Can you do an architecture sketch? Like if we pick Dedicated in eu-west-1, what are the data flows?
[05:02] Jordan Reyes: Sure — high level: customer app in eu-west-1 —> VPC peering or private link to Redwood Dedicated cluster in eu-west-1 —> requests served on dedicated GPUs —> logs shipped optionally to customer S3 or to Redwood but with redaction. We can send a diagram post-call.
[05:18] Emily Wong: About audit logs: regulators want immutable audit logs for certain actions and they have to live for seven years in some cases. Do you support WORM storage or can we forward logs to our retention system?
[05:28] Maya Patel: We don't provide WORM natively for Hosted; however, Dedicated/Private can forward logs to your S3 bucket where you can enforce WORM policies. Or we can integrate with your SIEM/ELK with guaranteed retention.
[05:42] Daniel Carter: Ok that helps. Timeline — target pilot in Q4, production next year. Stakeholders include legal, infra, security. We need procurement-friendly pricing and a security pack.
[05:54] Jordan Reyes: Understood. On procurement, do you have any prohibitions around third-party processors?
[05:58] Emily Wong: We prefer vendors who can sign our standard DPA and accept SCCs. Also, any subprocessors must be disclosed.
[06:06] Jordan Reyes: We provide subprocessors list and will include that in the docs we send.
[06:10] Mark Lewis: Two technical things: 1) can we run inference inside our VPC so that model never leaves? 2) What kind of metrics do you expose for token-level costs and latency?
[06:18] Maya Patel: 1) Private does that — full control. Dedicated also can be configured so the inference nodes sit in your VPC via a managed cluster, depending on cloud. 2) Our Console exposes per-route latency P50/P95/P99, per-token cost estimates, and trace hooks. We can also give you a CSV export for cost modeling.
[06:36] Daniel Carter: About logging restrictions: regulators sometimes forbid export of transaction metadata. Is metadata like request timestamps and user IDs considered sensitive?
[06:44] Maya Patel: It depends on your policy. We can treat user IDs as PII and mask them. Our logging pipeline supports field-level redaction — you can instruct us which fields to strip or hash before logs leave your environment.
[06:58] Emily Wong: On encryption keys, can Redwood rotate keys? We need to ensure rotation won't break access and that key rotation events are logged.
[07:06] Maya Patel: Yes, we support KMS rotation policies and will surface key rotation events. If you use customer-managed keys, you control rotation. We also support HSM for attestation for highest security needs.
[07:20] Jordan Reyes: Quick practical question: for the pilot, you'd probably want a small dedicated cluster in eu-west-1 with private link and logs forwarded to your account, correct?
[07:30] Daniel Carter: Likely. We want to validate PII handling and run a small eval with ~500 qps and typical prompts. If that goes well, scale to 2k qps.
[07:40] Maya Patel: Great — for benchmarking, we'll need sample prompts and expected sequence lengths. We'll propose batching and quantization options to meet cost/latency.
[07:52] Mark Lewis: Are there penalties for data egress across regions? We need to ensure no cross-border replication for EU data.
[07:58] Jordan Reyes: We can guarantee no cross-border replication for Dedicated/Private. Hosted can be configured but some features (like global caching) might replicate — we'd turn those off. We'll document replication behavior per feature.
[08:14] Emily Wong: Compliance docs — do you have SOC 2 Type II and pen test reports?
[08:18] Jordan Reyes: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II and recent penetration test summaries. We'll attach redacted reports.
[08:24] Daniel Carter: One more — logging retention policies: we need retention configurable to days, months, years depending on log type. Are retention policies per-bucket/per-route?
[08:34] Maya Patel: Retention is configurable per-log stream and per-customer. For Dedicated/Private you can use your S3 lifecycle policies for exact retention.
[08:44] Jordan Reyes: I'm also going to flag PCI — if you have cardholder data, we recommend not sending raw card numbers to any model.
[08:50] Mark Lewis: Yep we'll tokenise fields before sending.
[08:52] Daniel Carter: On the legal side, procurement will need subprocessors list and a BAA or DPA. Also our legal will want to see indemnification clauses for data breaches.
[09:02] Jordan Reyes: We'll share standard DPA/BAA language and mention subprocessors. For indemnities we can escalate to our legal — typical enterprise contracts are negotiable.
[09:12] Emily Wong: Anything special about model auditing? We need traceability of which model version served a request for reproducibility.
[09:18] Maya Patel: Absolutely — our console tracks model version, serving binary, and can attach a request ID to reproduce inference. For Dedicated/Private you can pin model versions.
[09:30] Daniel Carter: Can you support deletion of derivatively created data? If a user asks for erasure, we need to ensure any embeddings or vectors are removed.
[09:38] Maya Patel: We support vector store deletion and will scrub embeddings on request; we have an API endpoint for bulk erase that cascades to caches and storage with audit trail. We will include details in the whitepaper.
[09:56] Jordan Reyes: Quick note — sometimes transcripts we capture mislabel brand names, so apologies in advance if you see typos in the recorded notes.
[10:02] Daniel Carter: No worries. A few more nitty gritty items: 1) SSO/SAML for RBAC. 2) SCIM provisioning. 3) Fine-grained roles.
[10:12] Maya Patel: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC with custom roles on Dedicated/Private. Hosted supports RBAC too but with Redwood-managed identity unless you connect SSO.
[10:26] Mark Lewis: Anything about offline audits? Auditors sometimes want copies of logs. Do you provide read-only log exports?
[10:34] Maya Patel: Yes, we can export immutable snapshots or provide read-only access via temporary tokens to your auditors. For Dedicated/Private you can grant auditors direct bucket access.
[10:44] Emily Wong: Ok, cost question: relative to Hosted, how much more is Dedicated or Private? Ballpark percent?
[10:52] Jordan Reyes: Ballpark: Dedicated tends to be 2-4x hosted unit cost because you're paying reserved GPUs and isolation; Private can be similar to Dedicated plus deployment/ops fees. But with batching and cache tuning your per-token cost often drops for steady workloads. We'll provide a modeled estimate.
[11:12] Daniel Carter: We need a detailed RACI for the pilot: who manages upgrades, backups, compliance checks?
[11:20] Maya Patel: For Dedicated, Redwood manages the serving runtime and upgrades can be scheduled with you; backups and logs are typically managed by the customer if they're in your bucket. For Private, you manage upgrades unless you request Redwood-managed ops.
[11:34] Mark Lewis: About fallbacks — if capacity is constrained, can we auto-fail to a smaller model or to a hosted fallback?
[11:42] Maya Patel: Yes, our routing policies support fallbacks by model variant, region, or a degraded latency tier. Those policies are configurable.
[11:50] Emily Wong: Great. Any limitations around PII detection tools? We want integrated PII detection to mask before sending.
[11:58] Maya Patel: We have a PII detection pipeline that can run client-side via SDK or server-side with redaction rules. For highest control you can run detection client-side.
[12:10] Daniel Carter: Ok let's capture next steps and owners — I want security and procurement to review docs before the deep technical.
[12:18] Jordan Reyes: Perfect. We'll send a packet with SOC2/BAA/DPA, data residency whitepaper, architecture diagram, and initial pricing. Maya will schedule the deep technical.
[12:28] Daniel Carter: Sounds good. Anything else to cover?
[12:32] Mark Lewis: One minor: what's your SLA for P95 latency?
[12:36] Maya Patel: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed latency and uptime targets — we'll include specific numbers in the proposal. For Hosted there are uptime SLAs but latency SLAs vary by plan.
[12:48] Emily Wong: Ok thanks. We'll look for the packet.
[12:52] Jordan Reyes: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by end of week.
[12:56] Daniel Carter: Appreciate it.
[13:00] [End of recorded transcript — automated notes may contain mistakes. Full follow-up items captured separately.]
